query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a nanoscale graded refractory carbide/nitride interfacial coating on the tungsten surfaces in a W–Cu composite will suppress diffusion–driven phase separation and reduce the formation of interfacial voids, thereby improving thermal conductivity under high heat‐flux and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation during processing and service.
generation.intervention: Deposit a nanoscale graded refractory carbide/nitride layer on the tungsten surfaces prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions that include high-temperature consolidation and the service conditions of high heat flux and irradiation typical of joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded interfacial coating acts as a diffusion barrier and adhesion promoter, modifying the interfacial energy and reducing sites for void nucleation.
generation.mechanism: By limiting interdiffusion between W and Cu during high-temperature processing and irradiation, the coating suppresses phase separation. Its graded structure also enhances adhesion at the interface, thus reducing the nucleation and growth of voids, which in turn maintains or improves thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation, resulting in a measurable improvement in thermal conductivity relative to an untreated composite under similar high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite that develops phase separation and interfacial voids under equivalent processing and service conditions.
generation.boundary: Intervention efficacy is assumed within typical industrial-scale composite processing temperatures and exposure to irradiation and heat fluxes relevant to plasma-facing components and cooling joint environments.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the nanoscale coating under prolonged irradiation and thermal cycling is not fully established, which may affect performance over extended service durations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of similar W–Cu composites: one with the engineered nanoscale graded refractory carbide/nitride coating on tungsten surfaces and one without any coating. Process both sets under identical high-temperature consolidation conditions, then subject them to simulated service conditions including high heat flux and controlled irradiation exposure. After treatment, perform microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM and EDS) and thermal conductivity measurements.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of interfacial void area and phase separation via microscopy
Thermal conductivity tests (e.g., laser flash analysis)
Elemental diffusion profiles at the interface (EDS line scans)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composite with the nanoscale coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void formation and phase separation, or fails to demonstrate superior thermal conductivity compared to the uncoated composite under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
